meta.description: Genuine Dickens — but not advice. Jenny Wren says it in Our Mutual Friend (1864–65), Bk. 3 Ch. 2, defending Lizzie Hexam. The "Have a heart" opening is a re-cast.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Have a heart that never hardens, and a temper that never tires, and a touch that never hurts'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Dickens, wrong frame: it's Jenny Wren's line in Our Mutual Friend (1864–65), Bk. 3 Ch. 2 — a conditional defence of a friend, later re-cast as a maxim.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The triad is genuine Dickens: it appears in Our Mutual Friend, Book the Third, Chapter 2, serialised in monthly parts May 1864–November 1865 and published complete in 1865. One catch — Dickens wrote it as dialogue, not advice: the doll’s dressmaker Jenny Wren says “if it’s proud to have a heart that never hardens…” while defending her friend Lizzie Hexam, and the familiar imperative “Have a heart…” is a later re-cast of that conditional clause.

source.heading: The primary source

docMeta.dd: Book the Third (“A Long Lane”), Chapter 2 — “A Respected Friend in a New Aspect”
Serialised in monthly parts by Chapman and Hall, May 1864 – November 1865; published complete in 1865
Jenny Wren, the doll’s dressmaker, to Miss Abbey Potterson

source.excerpt:
“And if it’s proud to have a heart that never hardens, and a temper that never tires, and a touch that never hurts,” Miss Jenny struck in, flushed, “she is proud. And if it’s not, she is NOT.”

Her set purpose of contradicting Miss Abbey point blank, was so far from offending that dread authority, as to elicit a gracious smile. “You do right, child,” said Miss Abbey, “to speak well of those who deserve well of you.”
trail: Wikisource’s transcription of Book 3, Chapter 2 ↗ carries the line verbatim, in Jenny Wren’s mouth, immediately after Miss Abbey calls Lizzie Hexam proud.
A second, independent transcription at Victorian London ↗ matches word for word and continues into Miss Abbey’s reply, “You do right, child, to speak well of those who deserve well of you.”
Wikiquote ↗ lists the passage in its sourced quotations for Our Mutual Friend, giving the location as Bk. III, Ch. 2 — no dispute or misattribution flag attached.
The Dickens Project ↗ confirms the novel was issued by Chapman and Hall in monthly parts from May 1864 to November 1865, which fixes the first-publication date and the copyright status.
source.excerptNote: The “she” is Lizzie Hexam, whom Miss Abbey has just called “a very proud young woman.” Jenny does not deny the word — she redefines it.
source.rightsNote: Our Mutual Friend was first published in monthly parts between May 1864 and November 1865 and issued complete in 1865, far earlier than the 1931 cutoff, so the novel and this passage are in the public domain in the United States. The full text is freely available from Project Gutenberg ↗.

author.name: Charles Dickens
author.heading: Who was Charles Dickens?
author.bio: Charles Dickens (7 February 1812 – 9 June 1870) was an English writer and journalist who published almost all of his fiction in serial instalments, which is why his novels move in cliffhangers and crowds. Our Mutual Friend was the fourteenth and last novel he completed, a late, dark book about money, drowning and the Thames. Its most quoted sentence is not spoken by Dickens at all but by Jenny Wren, a disabled child who makes dolls’ dresses for a living and has the sharpest tongue in the book.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost in the quoting
misattribution.intro: Nobody is stealing this line from Dickens — the triad really is his. What travels badly is everything around it: who says it, what grammatical shape it had, and which book it came from.

items.why: Dickens wrote a conditional, not a command: “And if it’s proud to have a heart that never hardens, and a temper that never tires, and a touch that never hurts… she is proud. And if it’s not, she is NOT.” Dropping the “if it’s proud to” turns a piece of argument into a greeting-card instruction. See the passage in Wikisource ↗.

It is spoken by the doll’s dressmaker Jenny Wren, “flushed,” contradicting Miss Abbey Potterson to defend Lizzie Hexam — after which Miss Abbey smiles and says, “You do right, child, to speak well of those who deserve well of you.” The exchange is transcribed at Victorian London ↗.

items.who: The blessing form, “May you have a heart that never hardens…”
items.why: A benediction-shaped version circulates under Dickens’s name on quotation sites — for example this Goodreads entry ↗. Dickens wrote no such sentence; the “May you” frame is somebody else’s addition.

items.who: The line quoted with no speaker and no chapter
items.why: Even Dickens-focused sites reproduce the short imperative and name only the novel — the Charles Dickens Info quotations page ↗ lists it as “Have a heart that never hardens…” from Our Mutual Friend without identifying Jenny Wren or the chapter.

misattribution.truthLine: The three clauses are verbatim Dickens; the sentence they sit in is not. Wikiquote places the passage in its sourced section under Our Mutual Friend, Bk. III, Ch. 2 — see Wikiquote ↗.

context.heading: Why the line lands
lead: Miss Abbey Potterson, who runs the Six Jolly Fellowship Porters and rules it like a schoolmistress, has just called Lizzie Hexam “a very proud young woman.” It is meant as a criticism. Jenny Wren — small, disabled, a child who earns her living dressing dolls — will not let it stand, and instead of denying the charge she redefines it: if this is pride, then yes, Lizzie is proud.

That is what gives the sentence its spring. It is not a general-purpose maxim floating free; it is a rebuttal, delivered “flushed” by the least powerful person in the room to the most powerful, and it works — Miss Abbey smiles and concedes the point.
detailsBody: Our Mutual Friend was the last novel Dickens completed, serialised in monthly parts from May 1864 to November 1865 and issued complete in 1865, five years before his death.

The “she” of the passage is Lizzie Hexam, a waterman’s daughter whom the novel treats as its moral centre. Riah, the Jewish moneylender who has been protecting both Lizzie and Jenny, is present for the exchange.
context.pull: Dickens did not write it as advice. He wrote it as an argument, and the person making it wins.

sourcesVerified.claim: The exact wording "a heart that never hardens, and a temper that never tires, and a touch that never hurts" appears in Our Mutual Friend, Book 3, Chapter 2, spoken by Miss Jenny (Jenny Wren) in a conditional sentence beginning "And if it's proud to have..."
An independent transcription carries the same wording and the following line, Miss Abbey's reply: "You do right, child, to speak well of those who deserve well of you."
Wikiquote lists the passage in its sourced section for Our Mutual Friend, locating it at Bk. III, Ch. 2, and does not flag it as disputed or misattributed.

The chapter containing the line is Book the Third, Chapter 2, "A Respected Friend in a New Aspect," and Miss Abbey Potterson calls Lizzie Hexam "a very proud young woman" just before Jenny's interjection.
Our Mutual Friend was issued by Chapman and Hall in monthly parts from May 1864 to November 1865, in twenty parts published as nineteen numbers.

Our Mutual Friend is the fourteenth and final novel completed by Charles Dickens, serialised May 1864 to November 1865 and published in book form in 1865 by Chapman & Hall; Jenny Wren is a doll's dressmaker, Lizzie Hexam the novel's moral centre, Miss Abbey Potterson keeps the Six Jolly Fellowship Porters, and Riah is a Jewish moneylender who protects Lizzie and Jenny.
The complete text of Our Mutual Friend by Charles Dickens (1812-1870), originally published 1864-1865, is in the public domain in the USA and available as Project Gutenberg eBook 883.
Charles Dickens was an English writer and journalist, born 7 February 1812 and died 9 June 1870.

The full original sentence is circulated on quotation sites as "And if it's proud to have a heart that never hardens, and a temper that never tires, and a touch that never hurts,' Miss Jenny struck in, flushed, 'she is proud. And if it's NOT, she is NOT," sourced to Our Mutual Friend.
A benediction-form variant, "May you have a heart that never hardens, a temper that never tires, and a touch that never hurts," circulates attributed to Charles Dickens.

A Dickens-focused quotation site lists the line in its imperative short form, "Have a heart that never hardens, and a temper that never tires, and a touch that never hurts," sourced only to Our Mutual Friend with no speaker or chapter identified.
